domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core focus is agent design patterns including task decomposition, secondary-call error correction, Unix-style composability, and the latency trap in agentic systems. The talk is situated in financial workflows for investment professionals and involves building knowledge bases over large document corpora. The talk covers architecture design decisions and production deployment considerations including feedback loops and a live product demonstration. The talk assumes familiarity with LLMs, reinforcement learning, instruction tuning, and agent architecture concepts. This is a recorded conference presentation from the AI Engineer Summit 2025. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the transcript.

summary: Mike Conover, founder and CEO of Brightwave, discusses engineering and interaction design patterns for AI research agents in financial workflows. Brightwave digests large document corpuses for investment professionals facing tasks like pre-term sheet due diligence, earnings season coverage of 80-120 names, and confirmatory diligence across hundreds of vendor contracts. Conover draws a historical parallel to pre-1978 spreadsheet finance work, arguing knowledge agents will transform financial research by orders of magnitude. A central design challenge is revealing the thought process of a system that has considered 10,000+ pages in a useful, legible way—chat interfaces alone are likely insufficient. Conover observes non-reasoning models perform greedy local search, and chained calls with even 5% error rates compound exponentially. Winning systems will perform end-to-end RL over tool use calls, making locally suboptimal decisions for globally optimal outputs, though this remains an open research problem. He interprets multi-turn conversations as nudging activations in vector space toward problem-solving positions, and notes users won't invest ~1,000 hours becoming prompting experts, so verticalized product workflows will endure. For autonomous agent design, he advocates mimicking human decision-making: assess relevant documents, distill findings, then enrich and error-correct via secondary model calls, which outperform inline JSON chain-of-thought due to model credulity bias. He argues against anthropomorphizing agent components in favor of Unix-style composability with text as universal interface. The latency trap creates a time-to-value versus realized-value tradeoff requiring deliberate per-node tool selection. Synthesis is the core challenge: instruction tuning demonstrations have characteristic output lengths (even o1 outputs ~2,000-3,000 tokens), so large context windows create a compression problem. Decomposing research instructions into sub-themes yields higher-fidelity, information-dense outputs. Recombinative reasoning demonstrations are scarce in posttraining corpuses, limiting multi-document synthesis. Temporality remains hard—understanding M&A proforma statements and contract addendums requires propagating evidentiary metadata. The report is one view on a high-dimensional data structure; users need details on demand—clickable citations, highlightable passages, drill-down findings—and an audit trail of receipts. Human oversight remains essential because analysts possess non-digitized information like management conversations and portfolio manager taste.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Problem Space
sections.summary: Conover introduces Brightwave as a research agent for financial domains, describing high-stakes use cases: due diligence on thousands of data room pages, earnings season coverage of 80-120 names, and confirmatory diligence across hundreds of vendor contracts. He frames these as tasks beyond human-level intelligence given tight deadlines, noting junior analysts face impossible workloads.

sections.title: Background & Historical Parallel
sections.summary: Conover shares his background at Databricks creating Dolly, an early instruction-tuned open-source model. He draws a parallel to pre-1978 spreadsheet finance work, arguing AI tools will elevate analytical sophistication just as computational spreadsheets did. The talk's purpose is to share intelligence from building a high-fidelity research agent, including the design challenge of revealing reasoning across 10,000+ pages.

sections.title: Technical Challenges: RL, Error Compounding, and Model Behavior
sections.summary: Conover observes non-reasoning models perform greedy local search with compounding error in chained calls. Winning systems will perform end-to-end RL over tool use calls, though this is an open research problem. He interprets multi-turn conversations as nudging activations in vector space toward problem-solving positions, notes users won't become prompting experts (~1,000 hours), and predicts verticalized product workflows will endure.

sections.title: Agent Design Patterns & Error Correction
sections.summary: Conover outlines autonomous agent design patterns: mimic human decision-making by decomposing tasks—assess relevant documents, distill findings, enrich and error-correct. Secondary calls for error correction outperform inline JSON chain-of-thought because models are primed to be credulous about their own outputs. Human oversight is essential since analysts possess non-digitized information like management conversations and portfolio manager taste.

sections.title: Architecture Philosophy, Pareto Frontier & Latency Trap
sections.summary: Conover argues against anthropomorphizing agent components (portfolio manager agent, fact-checker) as it constrains flexibility, favoring Unix philosophy with text as universal interface. He discusses the shifting Pareto frontier for price-performance requiring deliberate per-node tool selection and introduces the latency trap: a time-to-value versus realized-value tradeoff in agentic systems, noting even high-quality products like OpenAI's Deep Research don't always deliver certainty.

sections.title: Synthesis Challenges, Output Limitations & Product Design
sections.summary: Conover explains synthesis as the core challenge: instruction tuning demonstrations have characteristic output lengths (even o1 outputs ~2,000-3,000 tokens), so large context windows create a compression problem. Decomposing research instructions into sub-themes yields higher-fidelity, information-dense outputs. Recombinative reasoning demonstrations are scarce in posttraining corpuses, limiting multi-document synthesis. Temporality remains hard—M&A proforma statements and contract addendums require propagating evidentiary metadata. He then demonstrates Brightwave's product: the report is one view on a high-dimensional data structure, with details-on-demand via clickable citations, highlightable passages, drill-down findings (fundraising timelines, litigation, patent disputes), and audit trails. Long feedback loops (8-20 minutes) limit user faculty with the system. He concludes that the final form factor for this product class has not yet been established and announces hiring.
